seed.relationship: a farmer and a surveyor from the city
seed.conflict: when someone returns after years without explaining
seed.topicSeed: a ferry terminal in Mumbai; a farmer and a surveyor from the city when someone returns after years without explaining

g.passage:
Diesel and wet rope, gulls quarrelling over fish heads—
I smell the harbor before I see you, Nikhil,
stepping off the noon ferry with your tripod
as if eleven years were a measurement you forgot to record.
I rehearsed this on the bus from the village:
how I would ask where you went, why no letter came
while my fields drowned and dried and drowned again.
I had sharpened every word like a sickle.
But you set the tripod down and kneel to tie my sandal,
the one whose strap has always slipped,
and your hands remember it.
So I, Rohan, who planned a harvest of questions,
stand quiet and let the terminal's loudspeaker
call out the names of other boats.

g.passage:
Manila, 1923. A barbershop on a narrow street, closed for the evening. WENHUA sweeps hair from the tiles. DEWI enters, holding a folded letter.
WENHUA: We are closed. Unless you have come to have your famous curls cut off at last—that, I would stay open for.
DEWI: You still talk like the second act. All sharp exits.
WENHUA: Someone had to have the good lines.
DEWI (setting the letter on the counter): I wrote this the week the company split. I never sent it.
(WENHUA stops sweeping. She does not touch the letter.)
WENHUA: I kept your fan. The painted one, from the opening night in Iloilo. I told myself I kept it to sell.
DEWI: Did you?
WENHUA (quietly): No buyer ever seemed right.
(She sets the broom against the mirror and pulls out the chair for DEWI.)

seed.topicSeed: a soccer field at dusk in Taipei; twin brothers dividing a house while waiting for important news

g.passage: Whistles thin as reeds, the thud of a ball on packed earth, the smell of rain held back in the clouds—such is the field at dusk in Taipei, where the twins Lanying and Salma came each evening to divide their late father's house. They did it on paper, at the edge of the pitch, as one might parcel out a kingdom: the east room to one, the cedar chest to the other, the courtyard well to be shared by a schedule no one would keep. Each line was argued with a lawyer's patience. Meanwhile a letter from the provincial court was expected, which would say whether the house could be kept at all. One evening the ball rolled to their bench, and Salma, without thinking, kicked it back to the boys with the old flick both twins had learned as children. Lanying laughed for the first time in weeks. The paper, I am told, was left on the bench that night and blew halfway across the field before anyone ran after it.

g.passage: I was then a schoolmaster in Surabaya, and Imtiaz, who had once called me Master Budi with real warmth, had not spoken to me since the term began. I had given him, before the holidays, a secondhand atlas, and he had taken it, I learned later, as a hint that his family's poverty kept him from seeing the world. He returned it wrapped in newspaper without a word. That spring the river rose and flooded the cellar beneath the schoolroom, where the old records were kept. I went down with a lamp, cursing the water, the cold, the ruined ledgers, the boy's stubborn pride, which seemed to me just another damp and useless thing. Then I heard splashing behind me. Imtiaz had followed, trousers rolled, and was lifting the drowned books one by one onto the steps, holding each to the light as if reading the names. We worked until the lamp ran dry, and neither of us needed to speak. The caretaker found us in the morning asleep on the stairs, the ledgers drying around us like laundry.

g.passage: Three rules hung on the laundromat wall in Moana's handwriting: no dyeing, no sleeping, no leaving wet clothes past closing. He had added a fourth in his head the day the will was read, a rule for himself: do not mention the chisel. His father had left the carving chisel, the one with the whalebone handle, not to Moana but to Moana's son, Tane, who was nineteen and wanted to fix engines. Now Tane sat on a dryer, turning the chisel over, while the machines thumped. "You want it," Tane said. "Take it." Moana said that was not how it worked. Tane said that was exactly how it worked, that he could hand it over in one second. Moana folded a towel twice and did not answer. Then he asked, almost against his will, whether Tane had ever noticed the small notch near the blade. Tane had not. Moana took the chisel, showed him where his own thumb had slipped at age eight, and handed it back. "Your grandfather wanted someone to ask about that," he said. Outside, a bus hissed at the stop, and the last dryer clicked off.

options: It describes a family quarrel over a chisel and then shows the son giving it up to end the dispute.
It lists the rules of a business and then explains why the father enforces them so strictly.

g.passage: Beirut in August is a city of waiting rooms, and the one on the third floor of the hospital smelled of oranges someone had peeled hours before. I had been there since dawn, rehearsing how I would tell my father that he could not go back to the harbor house alone. Across from me sat a man I half recognized. He said his name was Hamza and that, as a boy, he had crossed the bay every morning on my father's boat. "He let me steer once," he said, "and pretended not to see when I aimed for the rocks." I laughed despite myself. Hamza told me other things: how my father sang to the engine, how he gave free passage to anyone carrying bread. By the time the nurse called, "Noor?" I no longer meant to tell my father he must leave the harbor. I meant to ask him which of his passengers he would want to live near. In the corridor, a cart rattled past, stacked with folded white sheets.

g.passage: Smoke from the idling engines, the clang of a wrench dropped on stone, the sweet rot of mangoes in the gutter: such was the depot where I, Yusuf, went to find my grandfather's oldest friend. I went, I admit, as a prosecutor. My grandfather had always said that he and Esteban had both given up their passage to Spain so that a sick cousin might go instead, and I had come to believe Esteban had given up far less. He had stayed, after all, and prospered with his buses. I put the matter to him directly. Esteban did not defend himself. He took me to a cracked ledger in the dispatcher's office and showed me a column of small sums, paid every month for thirty years, marked only with my grandfather's initials. "He never knew where they came from," Esteban said. "I preferred it so." I walked home along the Malecón without my accusation. The sea that evening was the color of an old ledger's ink, and the boys were fishing from the wall.

options: The narrator voices a suspicion about past sacrifices and then finds evidence that overturns it.
The narrator describes a busy depot and then explains how buses replaced older forms of travel.

The narrator praises Esteban's generosity and then questions whether it was ever sincere.

g.passage: Why did Mio sit out the whole of that season, she who could outrun every girl in the district? So the village asked, and so I asked, as a child picking leaves on the slopes beyond Kyoto. Sachiko, who trained the runners for the autumn festival race, gave no reason. She only told Mio to rest, and Mio rested, sitting each morning among the tea rows while the others ran the hill road. People said the coach was jealous, or the girl was lazy. Years afterward, I learned what both had known: Mio's heart had a flutter that the doctor in town feared, and Mio's mother, a widow already burdened, had begged that no one speak of it. Sachiko had let herself be called jealous rather than say a word. I think of this whenever the tea bushes are trimmed in spring, their tops cut flat and even, so that no single branch stands above the rest.

g.passage: Four things lived in Jomo's back room: a treadle machine, a dressmaker's dummy with no head, a radio that caught only one station, and the runner-up plate from the 1979 district chess final, which he had lost and I had won. I was twelve then. Afterward, everyone said I had been brilliant to beat a grown man, and I had believed them for ten years. Now I sat on his cutting table while he hemmed a pair of trousers, and I asked, idly, why he kept the plate behind the radio instead of on the shelf. He did not answer at once. __He pinned the hem, then unpinned it, then pinned it again in exactly the same place.__ At last he said that my father had been ill that winter, and that he had wanted me to have something to be proud of that was not about my father. "You played well," he said. "I played worse on purpose." The radio announced the noon news, and a bus ground its gears in the street below.

g.passage: Yuto had been taught, in his first week as an apprentice, that no beam should cross a river unless the river had been watched through one full spring. Zhiming, the master carpenter, repeated the rule so often that Yuto came to think of it as weather, something simply true. Then came the dry summer, when the river below the village shrank to a bed of pale stones, and the farmers asked for a footbridge before the harvest. Yuto expected his master to refuse. Instead Zhiming walked the riverbed for an afternoon, turning over stones, pressing his palm to the cracked mud. __He came back with his sleeves gray to the elbow and said only that the river had been talking all along, if one knew where to listen.__ The bridge they built was low and short, pinned rather than nailed, so it could be lifted away. Yuto has kept the rule ever since, though he understands now that watching can take many forms. That autumn, the cranes returned to the fields early.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It indicates that Zhiming has fulfilled the rule's purpose through a different kind of watching.

It reveals that Zhiming, worn out by his search, no longer wishes to argue with the farmers.

g.passage: Seeds keep longer than people expect. Marit used to say this to every new member of the cooperative, tapping the glass jars along the warehouse shelves in Rotterdam: beans from 1961, a blue-podded pea no shop had sold in decades. When her son married Saga, Marit brought the bride to the warehouse the very next week and taught her to label envelopes in the old way: variety, grower, year. By then the lease was ending, and the members had stopped coming to meetings, but no one said the word closing. Saga learned quickly. __She began writing a fourth line on each envelope, in small letters: where it could be planted next.__ Marit noticed and said nothing for a month. Then, one wet afternoon, she handed Saga the key to the oldest cabinet and a list of gardens across the city, some of them belonging to people she had not spoken to in years. The last jars left in a borrowed van, rattling down the Maasboulevard in the rain.

g.passage: How long can a person avoid the woman who saw her cry on a crowded bus? For you, Nadeesha, the answer was eleven days. You took rickshaws to the ceramics studio instead, though they cost more than your clay. You told yourself Kamala, who had driven the number 6 for as long as you had ridden it, would have forgotten how you sobbed over a cracked bowl in your lap while the whole bus watched. Then, on the twelfth day, Kamala walked into the studio. She had signed up for the beginners' class. She sat at the wheel beside yours and made, with great concentration, a lopsided cup that collapsed. She laughed, loudly, at herself. You laughed too, and the room laughed with you, and the shame you had been carrying shrank to something that fit in a pocket. Not that you will admit this. You still claim the rickshaws were for the fresh air. Kamala's cup, refired, now holds your brushes.

Detached curiosity about the routines of a bus driver and her passengers
Uneasy sympathy for Nadeesha's financial strain in paying for rickshaws
g.explanation: 서술자는 Nadeesha가 점토값보다 비싼 릭샤를 타며 Kamala를 피한 일을 담담하면서도 장난스럽게 짚는다. 또 수치심이 주머니에 들어갈 만큼 작아졌다고 따뜻하게 묘사하면서, 지금도 신선한 공기 때문이라고 우긴다며 놀린다. 이 두 곳을 연결하면 애정 어린 놀림과 이해가 드러나므로 B가 정답이다. A의 엄격함, C의 무관심, D의 경제적 걱정은 서술자의 태도와 맞지 않는다.

seed.relationship: a boy and the old man who sells him fish

g.passage: On the morning the newspaper printed Shuang's drawing of the market, the boy came to Babatunde's stall before the fish had even been laid on the ice. The old man had sold him a single small fish every Saturday for three years, and on most Saturdays the boy had sketched the stall while he waited. Now the sketch was famous for a day, and strangers crowded the narrow lane to see the fish seller from the picture. Babatunde sold more than he had sold in a month; he also lost his quiet corner, his slow conversations, the boy's patient presence on the upturned crate, for Shuang could no longer sit there without being stared at. One should not pretend this was a tragedy. A man may complain of too many customers only so long before his neighbors stop listening. Yet one notices that Babatunde, counting his coins that evening, set aside the smallest fish in a twist of paper, as he always had, and waited past dark.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Babatunde's situation?
options: Open scorn for Babatunde's complaints about his sudden prosperity
Cheerful approval of the publicity that brought new customers to the market
Wry but tender sympathy for what the old man lost through his success
Solemn grief over the end of a friendship ruined by a newspaper
g.explanation: 서술자는 이것이 비극은 아니며 손님이 많다는 불평은 오래 들어 주지 않는다고 말해 상황을 살짝 비꼬듯 바라본다. 동시에 Babatunde가 조용한 자리와 소년의 존재를 잃었다고 나열하고, 저녁에 늘 그랬듯 작은 생선을 따로 챙겨 어두워질 때까지 기다리는 모습을 보여 준다. 두 부분을 함께 보면 냉소가 아닌, 재치 있으면서도 다정한 연민이 드러나므로 C가 정답이다. A는 경멸이 지나치고, B는 상실을 무시하며, D는 서술자가 비극이 아니라고 한 것과 충돌한다.

seed.conflict: over a recipe that was never written down
seed.topicSeed: a seaside promenade in the Cornish coast; a captain and a stowaway over a recipe that was never written down

g.passage:
Who measures salt by the sound it makes
falling into a pot? Soren did,
old captain, on the promenade bench,
explaining his fish stew to the gulls
and to Leah, who had once hidden
in his hold among the potato sacks
and been found, and fed, and never sent back.
A handful of this. Enough of that.
Until it smells like the harbor at Newlyn
the morning after a storm.
Such instructions are useless, of course.
No cook could follow them.
And still she leans close, notebook shut,
learning the way he tilts his wrist,
the pause he takes before the pepper,
as if the recipe were a weather
only the body could forecast.
Below them the tide pulls the sand smooth
and writes nothing on it either.
g.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward the way Soren's recipe is passed on?
options: Mild frustration that Soren refuses to record his recipe in exact amounts
Sentimental regret that the recipe will vanish once Soren is gone
Amused skepticism about whether Leah will ever master the stew
Affectionate respect for knowledge that passes by gesture, not writing
g.explanation: 화자는 소리로 소금을 재는 사람이 누구냐는 질문으로 시작해 Soren의 감각적인 요리법을 경이롭게 소개한다. '쓸모없는 지시'라고 인정하면서도 'And still' 이후 Leah가 공책을 덮은 채 손목의 기울기와 멈춤을 배우는 모습을 몸만이 예측하는 날씨에 비유한다. 이 두 부분을 연결하면 몸짓으로 전해지는 지식에 대한 애정 어린 존중이 드러나므로 D가 정답이다. A는 '쓸모없다'는 말만 보고 고른 오답이고, B와 C는 지문에 근거가 없다.

g.passage: "Ma'am, this was in the type case," said the boy who brings the paper stock, and he held out my husband's brass composing stick, which I had searched for since the funeral. I confess I was short with him. I believed, as widows are inclined to believe, that every hand in the press room of Port of Spain was waiting to carry off some piece of my husband's trade. Yet the boy did not leave. He asked, with a gravity beyond his years, whether the stick was set to the width of the Gazette or the hymn sheets, for he had noticed the measure was odd. No one but my husband had ever asked me such a question. I showed him. He set three lines of type, slowly and with many errors, and corrected each himself before I could point it out. My sister-in-law, Pearl, says I have taken a stray into the business. Perhaps I have. The boy comes at seven each morning now, and the composing stick is never where I left it, and I no longer search.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward the delivery boy?
options: Initial suspicion that gives way to grudging respect and warmth
Lasting distrust masked by polite gratitude for the boy's help
Pity for the boy's poverty mixed with impatience at his errors
Indifference toward the boy until Pearl insists that he be hired
g.explanation: 화자는 처음에 인쇄소의 모든 손이 남편의 물건을 노린다고 믿어 소년에게 퉁명스럽게 대했다고 고백한다. 그러나 소년이 남편만 하던 질문을 하고 스스로 오류를 고치는 모습을 본 뒤, 매일 아침 오는 그를 받아들이고 더 이상 막대를 찾지 않는다. 이처럼 의심이 마지못한 존중과 따뜻함으로 바뀌므로 A가 정답이다. B는 불신이 지속된다고 보았고, C의 동정이나 D의 무관심과 Pearl의 고용 강요는 지문에 근거가 없다.

seed.relationship: two neighbors with a shared wall
seed.conflict: over an invitation one of them refuses

g.passage: Three times Tendai invited me to supper, and three times I refused, each time with a reason that sounded better on the stair than it had in my head. We shared a wall, Tendai and I, in a narrow house near the Company's Garden, and through that wall I heard her sing while she cooked, badly and with great happiness. I told myself I was too busy. In truth I was a widow of one year, and a table set for two seemed to me a kind of trap. I took to spending evenings in the reading room of the public library, where silence was not only allowed but required. One night I looked up from my book and saw Tendai at the next table, reading a cookery manual with a pencil behind her ear. She did not invite me again. She only slid a slip of paper across the table: a list of dishes, with a question mark beside each. I have kept it, though I am ashamed to say how long I took to answer. The reading lamps in that room were green, and they hummed when the trams went by.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator Sunethra's attitude in the text?
options: Lingering resentment of Tendai for intruding on her private grief
Rueful self-awareness about her refusals and fondness for Tendai
Amused contempt for Tendai's poor singing and clumsy cooking
Proud satisfaction at having protected her solitude successfully
g.explanation: 화자는 거절 이유가 머릿속보다 계단에서 더 그럴듯하게 들렸다고 말하며, 사실은 2인용 식탁이 덫처럼 느껴졌다고 스스로를 돌아본다. 또 Tendai의 노래를 '서툴지만 아주 행복하게'라고 표현하고, 그녀가 건넨 쪽지를 간직하며 늦게 답한 것을 부끄러워한다. 이 단서들을 연결하면 자신의 거절에 대한 씁쓸한 자각과 Tendai에 대한 애정이 드러나므로 B가 정답이다. A의 원망, C의 경멸, D의 자부심은 화자의 태도와 맞지 않는다.

seed.relationship: a violin student and an exacting teacher

g.passage: Steam from the barley tea, the tick of the old refrigerator, the smell of rain on the volcanic stone outside: Jiwoo noticed all of it because she could not bear to notice the score on the table. Bruno had asked to see the sonata she had been composing for two years, and she had brought only the first movement, the one she had rewritten eleven times. He read it in silence. In lessons he was merciless about a single wavering note. Now he said only, "Where is the rest?" She told him it was not ready. He set the pages down and showed her his own notebook, its margins full of half-finished melodies dated decades back. "Neither was mine," he said. The landlady came in then, shaking out an umbrella, and set a bowl of tangerines by the sink.
g.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To recount a lesson in which Bruno corrects the errors in Jiwoo's first movement
To describe the atmosphere of a rainy boarding-house kitchen on Jeju Island
To suggest that every artist must eventually abandon some creative work
To show a demanding teacher easing a student's fear of sharing unfinished work
g.explanation: 앞부분에서 Jiwoo는 악보를 차마 보지 못하고 1악장만 열한 번 고쳐 가져올 만큼 미완성 작품을 보여 주기를 두려워한다. 뒷부분에서 평소 흔들리는 음 하나에도 가차 없던 Bruno는 수십 년 된 미완성 선율로 가득한 자신의 공책을 보여 주며 '내 것도 그랬다'고 말한다. 이 대비를 통해 엄격한 스승이 학생의 두려움을 덜어 주는 장면임이 드러나므로 D가 정답이다. A는 실제로 교정하지 않으므로 틀리고, B는 배경 묘사에 그치며, C는 지나치게 일반적인 교훈이다.
